entry.title: Risk of cardiovascular events and mortality associated with LDL and non-HDL cholesterol levels after statin initiation for primary prevention: A multiregional cohort study

link.title: Risk of cardiovascular events and mortality associated with LDL and non-HDL cholesterol levels after statin initiation for primary prevention: A multiregional cohort study
(PDF) Risk of cardiovascular events and mortality associated with LDL and non-HDL cholesterol levels after statin initiation for primary prevention: A multiregional cohort study
(XML) Risk of cardiovascular events and mortality associated with LDL and non-HDL cholesterol levels after statin initiation for primary prevention: A multiregional cohort study

entry.content:
by Joseph Edgar Blais, Ralph Kwame Akyea, William Harrison, Amy Hai Yan Chan, Wenfang Zhong, Stephen Franklin Weng, Kebede Abera Beyene, Wallis C. Y. Lau, Kenneth K. C. Man, Nadeem Qureshi, Esther Wai Yin Chan, Ian Chi Kei Wong, Jeff Harrison

Background

The cardiovascular and mortality benefits of achieving guideline-recommended concentrations of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and non-high-density lipoprotein (non-HDL) cholesterol with statins in primary prevention remain uncertain.

Methods and findings

In this new-user cohort study, we used electronic healthcare databases from Hong Kong (HK), New Zealand (NZ) and the United Kingdom (UK) to identify 185,237 patients initiating statins between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2012 (with follow-up to 31 December 2017) without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease. Associations between LDL and non-HDL cholesterol measured within 2 years post-initiation with the outcomes of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) or all-cause mortality were assessed in landmark analyses using multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, obesity, smoking, alcohol misuse, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus and connective tissue disorders, severe mental illness, antihypertensive drugs, antidiabetic drugs, antiplatelet drugs, and anticoagulant drugs. Estimates were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis. At 2 years, LDL cholesterol was <1.4 mmol/L in 7,084 (3.8%), 1.4–1.7 mmol/L in 21,893 (11.8%), 1.8–2.5 mmol/L in 81,941 (44.2%) and ≥2.6 mmol/L in 74,294 (40.1%) patients. Mean duration of follow-up for the primary outcome of MACE was 6.5 years in HK, 5.6 years in NZ and 5.4 years in UK. versus an LDL cholesterol ≥2.6 mmol/L, adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for MACE were 0.80 (95% CI [0.77,0.83]) for 1.8–2.5 mmol/L, 0.79 (0.66,0.94) for 1.4–1.7 mmol/L and 0.82 (0.60,1.12) for <1.4 mmol/L. Non-HDL cholesterol showed similar estimates for MACE (e.g., HR 0.75, [0.72,0.79] for 2.6–3.3 mmol/L versus ≥3.4 mmol/L). In continuous analysis, the association with MACE was approximately log-linear across achieved LDL and non-HDL cholesterol in HK and the UK, whereas in NZ estimates were less consistent and imprecise at the lowest concentrations. After adjustment for confounding factors, very low LDL (HR 1.06, [0.96,1.16]) and non-HDL cholesterol (HR 0.98, [0.84,1.14]) were not associated with all-cause mortality. Limitations include heterogeneity across cohorts, which may reflect confounding by indication where treatment intensity was guided by cardiovascular risk, and residual confounding from comorbidities, lifestyle interventions and disease severity. Estimates are also conditional on patients having initiated statins, survived to the landmark, and undergone follow-up lipid testing.

Conclusions

Lower achieved LDL and non-HDL cholesterol after statin initiation was associated with a reduction in MACE, with limited evidence of an increase in all-cause mortality at very low concentrations after adjustment for confounding. Additional reductions in cardiovascular events could be obtained by achieving guideline-recommended non-HDL cholesterol levels of at least <3.4 mmol/L after statin initiation for primary prevention.

entry.title: Transforming pandemic influenza antiviral stockpiling using a capacity-based approach: A modeling study

link.title: Transforming pandemic influenza antiviral stockpiling using a capacity-based approach: A modeling study
(PDF) Transforming pandemic influenza antiviral stockpiling using a capacity-based approach: A modeling study
(XML) Transforming pandemic influenza antiviral stockpiling using a capacity-based approach: A modeling study

entry.content:
by Nir Gavish, Amit Huppert

Background

Pandemic influenza preparedness in high-resource nations has traditionally relied on large antiviral stockpiles, typically targeting coverage for 25% of the population. This inventory-based benchmark focuses on cumulative disease burden but often overlooks the inelastic capacity of healthcare systems to manage acute surges. As multi-billion-dollar inventories reach expiration, we evaluated whether static stockpiles remain a viable strategy for preventing healthcare system collapse during future pandemics.

Methods and findings

We projected daily hospital bed demand using three complementary frameworks: a static lower-bound estimation, a dynamic deterministic Susceptible-Infectious-Hospitalized-Recovered transmission model, and historical reconstructions of the 1918, 1957, and 1968 pandemics using mortality data. We evaluated official planning scenarios for the United Kingdom, Japan, and the United States, comparing projected demand against national surge capacities (i.e., staffed beds). To test the theoretical limits of the stockpile strategy, we applied best-case assumptions, including perfect distribution of antivirals to 100% of symptomatic cases and high clinical effectiveness (30% to 60% reduction in hospitalization).Our models identified a critical feasibility gap. While stockpiles successfully suppressed demand to manageable levels in moderate scenarios (analogous to 1957/1968), they were structurally insufficient for severe events. In high-severity scenarios (analogous to 1918 or CDC Very Severe parameters), the daily surge of patients exceeded available hospital capacity by a factor of 5–9. This inundation occurred even under the assumption of 100% treatment coverage, rendering antivirals incapable of preventing transition to crisis standards of care. Although this analysis is subject to the inherent uncertainties of future pandemics, our use of optimistic best-case assumptions suggests that the identified structural failures are a lower-bound estimate. Realistic operational hurdles would only widen the disparity between stockpile targets and system capacity.The main limitations of this study’s methodology are its inherent optimistic bias, specifically the use of a conservative 4-day hospital length of stay that underestimates prolonged intensive care needs, the reliance on general hospital beds as a proxy that abstracts away from critical sub-system bottlenecks, and the assumption of guaranteed antiviral efficacy against novel strains.

Conclusions

This study demonstrates that large reserves cannot overcome the rigid physical constraints of healthcare systems, even under the optimistic assumption of perfect distribution. Consequently, the conventional 25% coverage target for antiviral stockpiles, a hallmark of legacy planning, presents a critical opportunity for re-evaluation. As global stocks near expiration, policymakers are uniquely positioned to leverage this inflection point by exploring a capacity-based framework. This adaptive paradigm suggests incorporating a synergistic mix of targeted reserves, temporary non-pharmaceutical interventions, and flexible delivery options, such as decentralized home-first care. Together, these integrated measures could serve as a vital temporal bridge, preserving system integrity until vaccine deployment.

entry.content:
by Susanna Tall, Maaret Turtinen, Anna Parviainen, Jenni Pettersson, Anna But, Taina Härkönen, Jussi Hepojoki, Tarja Sironen, Rommel Iheozor-Ejiofor, Hasan Uğurlu, Kalle Saksela, Jorma Ilonen, Suvi M. Virtanen, Olli Vapalahti, Mikael Knip, on behalf of the Finnish Pediatric Diabetes Register

Background

While COVID-19 lockdowns have been systematically associated with increased incidence rate of type 1 diabetes, less is known about the disease rates after lockdowns. We compared the incidence of type 1 diabetes after the COVID-19 pandemic-related closure of society (i) to the time when lockdown was implemented and to (ii) the time before the pandemic in Finland.

Methods and findings

The incidence of type 1 diabetes after the lockdown (09/2021–12/2022) was compared to the incidence during the lockdown (03/2020–08/2021) and before the lockdown (three 18-month terms 2014–2019) in Finnish children under the age of 15 years. Previous exposure to SARS-CoV-2 was identified by combining information on COVID-19 vaccination with data on SARS-CoV-2 antibodies analyzed in blood samples. The temporal cohort included 3,467 pediatric type 1 diabetes cases, distributed across post-lockdown (n = 586), lockdown (n = 785), and pre-pandemic (n = 2,096) periods. The incidence of type 1 diabetes after the lockdown was significantly lower than the incidence during the lockdown [incidence rate ratio (IRR = 0.85; 95% Cl [0.77,0.95]; p = 0.004)]. The rate of type 1 diabetes after the lockdown did not significantly differ from the time before lockdown (IRR = 1.00; 95% Cl [0.91,1.09]; p = 0.932). The frequency of children testing positive for infection-associated SARS-CoV-2 antibodies increased from 0.9% during the lockdown to more than 40% after the lockdown. Study limitations include a relatively short follow-up period after the lockdown and the lack of explicit modeling of the underlying long-term secular trend in type 1 diabetes incidence.

Conclusions

The lockdown represents a peak in childhood type 1 diabetes incidence in Finland compared to both the pre-pandemic and post-lockdown periods. However, the reversion toward historical levels after the lockdown does not necessarily establish a return to the expected historical trajectory, nor can it fully distinguish a transient change from temporal compensation superimposed on the background secular trend. The contrasting patterns between type 1 diabetes incidence and SARS-CoV-2 antibody prevalence during and after the lockdown suggest an indirect rather than a direct role of the virus in triggering the observed changes in incidence.

entry.content:
by Jeromie Wesley Vivian Thangaraj, Padinjaremattathil Thankappan Ullas, Balaji Dagadu More, Lokesh Shanmugam, Saravanakumar Velusamy, Dinesh Gopal, Subashri Ramamoorthy, Kanagasabai Kaliaperumal, Mugunthan N. M, Sandhya Arunachalam, Ramaprabha Ramachandran, Gopinath Ramakrishnan, Suresh Arunachalam, Vijay Vidhyakar J. M, Ganeshnee Anthuvan Valli, Siddharth Pugalendhi, Sabarinathan Ramasamy, Karunakaran T, Mohamed Hanifah, Sam Joy, Anoop Velayudhan, Suganya Egambaram, Ala Saritha, Manju Rahi, Simmi Tiwari, Vijay Parashramji Bondre, Manoj V. Murhekar, the Rabies Vaccine Immunogenicity Trial (RVIT) study group

Background

Shorter rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens could improve compliance and access by reducing the number of clinic visits and vaccine requirement per patient. We compared the immunogenicity and safety of a 1-week intradermal Institut Pasteur du Cambodge (IPC) regimen with a 1-month intradermal Updated Thai Red Cross regimen (UTRC) using two rabies vaccines widely used in India: Purified Chick Embryo Cell vaccine (PCECV) and the Purified Vero Cell Rabies vaccine (PVRV).

Methods and findings

We conducted a phase 4, single-centre, open-label randomised controlled equivalence trial among adult healthy volunteers. Participants were block randomised (1:1:1:1) to receive either the IPC (Days 0, 3, 7) or UTRC (Days 0, 3, 7, 28) intradermal regimen with either PCECV or the PVRV. Rabies virus neutralizing antibody (RVNA) titres were measured up to 1 year. The primary objective of the trial was to determine the immunogenicity of the Intradermal abridged Cambodia regimen with updated intradermal Thai red cross regimen using two different vaccine types among healthy volunteers in India. The primary outcome was geometric mean concentration ratios (GMR) of RVNA on day 42, assessed separately for each vaccine type. Equivalence for each vaccine was predefined as the entire 95% confidence interval for GMR lying between 0.72 and 1.04. The secondary outcomes included proportion of participants with RVNA titres >= 0.5 IU/mL on Days 14, 28, 42, 90, 180, and 365 and vaccine safety. Between October 10, 2023, and December 23, 2023, 400 participants were randomly assigned (100 per group) to PCECV-IPC, PCECV-UTRC, PVRV-IPC, and PVRV-UTRC. 362 (90.5%) completed PEP regimen and blood draw on day 42. In the prespecified modified intention-to-treat analysis, the Day 42 GMR (IPC vs UTRC) was 0.59 (95% CI: 0.47–0.75) for PCECV and 0.76 (95% CI: 0.61–0.95) for PVRV, which did not meet the prespecified equivalence criterion. All participants, irrespective of baseline serostatus, in four groups had RVNA titres ≥0.5 IU/ml at every assessment from day 14–1 year. Adverse events were similar between regimens and mostly mild. There are important limitations in this study. Nearly one-quarter of participants had baseline RVNA titres ≥0.5 IU/mL despite exclusion of participants with a reported history of rabies vaccination or dog bite, suggesting unrecognised prior immunological priming that may have influenced GMC estimates. As the trial was conducted among healthy volunteers rather than people receiving PEP after animal bites, the findings may not fully reflect vaccine performance in routine post-exposure settings.

Conclusion

The IPC regimen did not meet the prespecified equivalence criterion compared to UTRC. All participants achieved RVNA titres ≥0.5 IU/ml indicative of seroprotection from day 14 till 1 year. Policy decisions regarding replacement of UTRC should consider these immunogenicity findings together with compliance, cost, and vaccine availability.

Trial Registration

The trial was registered with the Clinical Trial Registry – India (CTRI/2023/10/058418). URL: https://ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=OTAxMDA=&Enc=&userName=).

entry.title: Challenges and recommendations for implementation of oncology clinical practice guidelines in China

link.title: Challenges and recommendations for implementation of oncology clinical practice guidelines in China
(PDF) Challenges and recommendations for implementation of oncology clinical practice guidelines in China
(XML) Challenges and recommendations for implementation of oncology clinical practice guidelines in China

entry.content:
by Minzhi Lv, Duanduan Yuan, Yue Suo, Fang Ding, Lijuan Hu, Lei Cao, Yi Wang, Jing Lei, Shenglan Tang, Tianshu Liu

Summary points

As China’s cancer burden continues to rise and treatment becomes increasingly complex, clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are crucial to standardising cancer care and supporting clinical decision-making. Over the past decades, China has made substantial progress in developing oncology CPGs, transitioning from expert consensus and international adaptation toward domestically led guideline production.This Policy Forum presents an analysis of the optimisation and implementation of oncology CPGs in China. We argue that the core challenge facing oncology CPGs in China is not a lack of guidelines, but the absence of an integrated governance and implementation ecosystem, and insufficient alignment with local evidence.By situating China's oncology sector within a macro-health-system perspective, this Policy Forum provides a conceptual blueprint for other transition economies experiencing a mismatch between rapid clinical technology scaling and fragmented regulatory governance.We propose a four-part strategic framework: (1) Establishing a national joint clearinghouse and registration system; (2) integrating resource-stratified pathways with locally relevant evidence; (3) expanding free, diversified dissemination channels; and (4) embedding implementation science alongside healthcare financing alignment.Addressing these systemic gaps offers scalable lessons for global health systems aiming to transition from the quantity-driven expansion of clinical guidelines to equity-oriented, system-integrated quality enhancement.

entry.title: Cost-effectiveness of recommended interventions for managing low back pain: A systematic review

link.title: Cost-effectiveness of recommended interventions for managing low back pain: A systematic review
(PDF) Cost-effectiveness of recommended interventions for managing low back pain: A systematic review
(XML) Cost-effectiveness of recommended interventions for managing low back pain: A systematic review

entry.content:
by Stephanie Mathieson, Martin Underwood, Muhammad Ibrahim, Zhilin Hua, Zhaohua Zhu, Paulo H. Ferreira, Hema Mistry, Emily R. Atkins, Jocelyn L. Bowden, Jillian P. Eyles, Andrew M. Briggs, David J. Hunter, Manuela L. Ferreira

Background

Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. Although numerous treatment approaches are recommended by international clinical guidelines, there is still limited understanding of which interventions provide the best value for money. We aimed to critically appraise and summarise the evidence on the cost-effectiveness and costs of interventions endorsed in recent guidelines to manage low back pain (LBP), compared to usual care.

Methods and findings

We searched 10 electronic databases (e.g., MEDLINE (OvidSP), EMBASE (OvidSP), PsycINFO (OvidSP)) from inception to 9th of February 2026 for cost-effectiveness studies of guideline-recommended treatments to manage non-specific LBP. The primary outcome was cost/quality-adjusted life year (QALY), which was converted to 2024 Great British Pound values, tabulated and summarised qualitatively. Secondary outcomes were direct costs (total, interventional, health service use, community services and out-of-pocket costs) and indirect costs (e.g., lost wages, lost productivity, absenteeism). We assessed methodological quality using the Consensus Health Economics Criteria (CHEC) checklist for within-trial economic evaluations or the Philips checklist for modelling studies. Our review included 20 studies (17 within-trial economic evaluations and three modelling studies), published between 2005 and 2026. Half (n = 10) focussed on chronic LBP (>3-month duration), and eight included mixed populations (i.e., acute, subacute and chronic). All studies were of non-pharmacological, non-surgical interventions, both single-modality and multimodal interventions (e.g., exercise plus spinal manipulation; diet plus physical activity). Most interventions are cost-effective at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000. Moreover, interventions aiming to reduce fear and stress or support self-management in people with chronic LBP, as well as clinician-delivered interventions including yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy and self-management support are potentially cost-saving from the healthcare, societal and payer’s perspectives, as they are both more effective and less costly than usual care (e.g., first contact management, including advice and medication). All of the evidence is derived from high-income countries, and from a considerable heterogenous body of literature. Evidence on cost-effective treatments in low- and middle-income countries remains limited.

Conclusions

Non-pharmacological, non-surgical interventions that include education, psychological support, acupuncture and exercise seem to be cost-effective for managing LBP, compared to usual care. Improved access to and implementation of these effective treatments is urgently needed so more people can benefit from them in routine care.

Registration

The review was registered on PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk; CRD42024510270).

entry.title: Co-exposure to planned power outages and wildfire PM<sub>2.5</sub> and acute healthcare utilization in California: A time-stratified case-crossover study

link.title: Co-exposure to planned power outages and wildfire PM<sub>2.5</sub> and acute healthcare utilization in California: A time-stratified case-crossover study
(PDF) Co-exposure to planned power outages and wildfire PM<sub>2.5</sub> and acute healthcare utilization in California: A time-stratified case-crossover study
(XML) Co-exposure to planned power outages and wildfire PM<sub>2.5</sub> and acute healthcare utilization in California: A time-stratified case-crossover study

entry.content:
by Lauren Blair Wilner, Caitlin G. Jones-Ngo, Chen Chen, Bethany Kwoka, Vivian Do, Joel D. Kaufman, Laura C. Myers, Tarik Benmahrnia, Joan A. Casey

Background

To prevent wildfires, electric utilities may preemptively de-energize power lines (public safety power shutoffs [PSPS]). These PSPS events may unintentionally harm health, particularly for those with pre-existing conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or who rely on electricity-dependent medical equipment. Health impacts may worsen further if a wildfire occurs despite the power shutoff. To assess the effect of PSPS events, wildfire fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure, and their co-occurrence on cause-specific healthcare utilization.

Methods and findings

We identified PSPS events in California from 2013 to 2019, categorizing magnitude based on number of people without power by zip code. We leveraged zip code-level average daily wildfire PM2.5 estimates and respiratory, COPD-specific, cardiovascular, and psychiatric emergency department visits and unscheduled hospital admissions among adults aged 20+ from the California Department of Health Care Access and Information. Using a time-stratified case-crossover design, we estimated the impact of same-day and lagged PSPS events alone, wildfire PM2.5 alone, and their co-occurrence on healthcare utilization, adjusting for daily temperature.Severe PSPS events were associated with elevated odds of same-day respiratory encounters (OR = 1.06, 95% CI: 1.02, 1.11) and lag0–3 effects were similar. These associations were stronger for COPD. Compared to no PSPS or wildfire exposure, joint PSPS and 10 μg/m3 higher wildfire PM2.5 was associated with higher odds of respiratory encounters (1.16 [95% CI: 1.10, 1.22]), with evidence of multiplicative interaction. Associations were null for cardiovascular and psychiatric encounters.Limitations include exposure misclassification, because we assigned exposure at the residential zip code level, aggregating circuit-level data and not accounting for individual behavior or the potential for PSPS events to impact wildfire PM2.5 exposure.

Conclusions

PSPS events may increase risk of respiratory events requiring acute care utilization, especially when they co-occur with wildfire PM2.5.

by Katarzyna Starowicz, on behalf of the PLOS Medicine Staff Editors

Breast cancer treatment using systemic therapies has often focussed on remission and survival, but can cause severe side effects that negatively impact patient quality of life and function, sometimes with limited clinical benefit. In the era of precision oncology, one of the greatest opportunities may not be in identifying more patients for treatment, but rather in identifying those who can safely receive less to avoid overtreatment. Breast cancer treatment using systemic therapies can cause severe side effects that negatively impact patient quality of life and function, sometimes with limited clinical benefit. In this Editorial, Katarzyna Starowicz discusses how precision oncology tools may help us identify those who can safely reduce therapy to avoid overtreatment.

entry.title: Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study

link.title: Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study
(PDF) Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study
(XML) Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study

entry.content:
by Benjamin J. Singer, Alec Gleason, Isabella Impalli, Mikkel D. Nagorsen, Chungman Chae, Lauren C. Granskog, Philip C. Lee, Ramanan Laxminarayan, Joseph A. Lewnard

Background

Human antibiotic use is widely believed to contribute to the evolution and maintenance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens. While antibiotic stewardship should thus discourage use in situations where AMR-related harms outweigh clinical benefit, evidence to inform this assessment of tradeoffs is lacking, most notably in low-resource settings where gaps in antibiotic access persist. Quantitative understanding of use-resistance relationships is thus necessary as countries navigate commitments from the 2024 UN General Assembly resolution to reduce AMR burden by 2030.

Methods and findings

We used global surveillance data on AMR prevalence from 2000 to 2018 representing over 30 million bacterial isolates from 114 countries, along with antibiotic consumption estimates for each country and year, to estimate elasticity relationships between AMR and antibiotic exposure. Our analyses addressed 16 bacterial pathogens and antibiotic consumption across 7 drug classes, controlling for country-level health and development indicators via weighted regression models. Across pathogens, evidence that AMR is associated with population-level antibiotic exposure is strongest for Acinetobacter spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli. In a modeled counterfactual scenario, we estimate that 10% lower levels of antibiotic use, in comparison to current levels, across classes, would be associated with 38,000 (95% confidence interval: 36,000–41,000) fewer annual deaths attributable to AMR globally. Although substantial, this total represents only 0.50% of estimated bacterial disease mortality. In sub-Saharan Africa, where risk of death due to bacterial disease is greatest, the modeled avertible burden of AMR-attributable deaths comprises only 0.34% of bacterial disease mortality. Key limitations of the study include reliance on ecological relationships to infer modifiable burden, and under-representation of low-resource settings in surveillance data on antibiotic consumption and AMR.

Conclusions

Our findings suggest near-term achievable reductions in AMR-attributable deaths may be modest relative to the persisting burden of bacterial disease mortality. These estimates should inform assessments of the potential benefits and harms of restrictive versus permissive antibiotic use paradigms in epidemiologically distinct settings.

entry.title: Outcomes of home-based versus facility-based care for mild diphtheria during a large epidemic in Kano State, Nigeria: A retrospective matched cohort study

(PDF) Outcomes of home-based versus facility-based care for mild diphtheria during a large epidemic in Kano State, Nigeria: A retrospective matched cohort study

entry.content:
by Jonathan Polonsky, Suleiman Hudu, Khadidja Uthman, Yves Katuala, Philip Eghosa Evbuomwan, Hashim Juma Omer Osman, Abdulwahab Kabir Sulaiman, Ichola Ismael Adjaho, Cheick Oumar Doumbia, Etienne Gignoux, Franck Ale

Background

During Nigeria’s largest recorded diphtheria epidemic (first notified on 1 December 2022; more than 40,000 confirmed cases by January 2026), hospital capacity in Kano State was overwhelmed. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) introduced home-based care (HBC) for patients with mild disease; we asked whether mortality, long-term sequelae, and household transmission differed between HBC and care in a diphtheria treatment centre (DTC).

Methods and findings

We conducted a retrospective matched cohort study using MSF registry data and household interviews to compare mortality, long-term sequelae, and household transmission between patients with mild diphtheria treated under HBC or in a DTC. The primary outcomes were mortality, long-term sequelae, and household transmission. Mild diphtheria cases notified between January 2023 and January 2024 were exactly matched by treatment modality (HBC or DTC) on sex, age group, vaccination status, and ward of residence, and interviewed between September and October 2024, a median of 421 days after notification. Conditional logistic regression, adjusted for age, vaccination status, and treatment delay, was used to estimate the association between treatment modality and mortality, with robustness checked with propensity score weighting and sensitivity analyses. Of the 986 originally sampled patients, 491 (49.8%) were interviewed; with 178 replacements (substitute patients of similar age, sex, vaccination status, and area, interviewed when an originally selected patient could not be), 669 patients (362 HBC, 307 DTC) were analysed. After adjustment, mortality was lower with HBC than DTC care, but the interval included 1 (odds ratio [OR] 0.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.12,1.07]; p = 0.066); treatment delay was associated with increased mortality (OR 1.29 per day, 95% CI [1.00,1.67]; p = 0.048). Adding calendar time gave a similar estimate (OR 0.35, 95% CI [0.08,1.57]; p = 0.170). Vaccination was associated with lower odds of death (OR 0.32, 95% CI [0.10,0.98]; p = 0.047). HBC was not associated with increased household transmission or long-term sequelae. Residual confounding by disease severity, the small number of deaths (24), and replacement patients limit these findings.

Conclusions

Vaccination and early treatment were associated with survival; care setting was not clearly associated. When supported by clinical triage and structured follow-up, decentralised care may be an option to manage mild cases during diphtheria epidemics in settings with constrained hospital capacity.

entry.content:
by Daniel T. Tardo, Sanjay Sharma

Sudden cardiac death in the young is often due to silent inherited cardiac conditions. Although evidence increasingly supports cardiac screening as a preventative strategy, policies and frameworks differ globally. Structured screening frameworks that utilise AI-enabled technologies show great potential for enhancing disease detection and risk prediction. In this Perspective, Daniel Tardo and Sanjay Sharma discuss evidence that supports cardiac screening in the young as a preventative strategy for cardiovascular disease and sudden cardiac death. They highlight the need for structured screening frameworks, and discuss the potential of AI-enabled technologies for disease detection and risk prediction.

entry.content:
by Yonatan H. Grad, Rachel Mittelstaedt, Remco P. H. Peters

Summary points

The 2026 WHO guidelines recommending doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) represent the first global antibiotic prophylaxis recommendation for bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with provisions for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring.Doxy-PEP should be governed as an adaptive intervention subject to periodic, transparent review, but establishing decision rules faces challenges.Doxy-PEP is expected to select for resistance, including in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Staphylococcus aureus, and the gut and skin microbiomes; the scope of clinical consequences is incompletely understood.As STI prevalence falls, the benefit per dose declines while the AMR externality per dose is expected to grow, shifting the cost-benefit balance in ways that vary across populations and settings.Attributing changes in disease prevalence or resistance patterns to doxy-PEP is methodologically difficult, given incompletely understood and complex drivers of pre-existing trends, surveillance limitations, and heterogeneous uptake, raising questions about study designs, data sources, eligibility criteria, and governance mechanisms.A full accounting of benefits and harms is broader than reduced bacterial STI incidence and AMR. Benefits include consideration of patient-centered outcomes such as reduced anxiety regarding STI acquisition, avoidance of repeated treatment visits, and fewer STI-related complications. Harms include drug side effects, such as gastrointestinal adverse effects and concerns about use in pregnancy.

by Xiangji Ying, Tianjing Li, Joanne E. McKenzie, Matthew J. Page, Kiran Ninan, Jean-Pierre Oberste, Colby J. Vorland, Andrew W. Brown, Riaz Qureshi, Nicholas J. DeVito, Ian J. Saldanha, Martin Offringa, Nancy J. Butcher, Sirui Zhang, Phi-Yen Nguyen, Joe Menke, Veronica Ka Wai Lai, Halil Kilicoglu, Evan Mayo-Wilson

Background

Defining outcomes completely before conducting clinical trials helps to mitigate concerns about reporting biases; however, there is limited guidance to help investigators define outcomes completely.

Methods

Building on a previous framework, we developed guidance for defining trial outcomes completely and consistently. We reviewed literature, developed preliminary guidance, and refined guidance iteratively through pilot testing. We randomly selected 225 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from ClinicalTrials.gov, which evaluated 3,424 outcomes. Two raters followed a structured approach to define each outcome. When raters encountered outcomes they could not define, we refined our guidance. We continued this process until no further changes were needed. We finalized the guidance through multiple drafts and discussions among authors.

Findings

In clinical trials, a completely defined outcome includes six elements: outcome domain, specific measurement, specific metric, cutoff (if applicable), variable type, and time point. We developed guidance for naming specific measurements for both subjective and objective outcomes. We expanded on prior work by describing more comprehensive categories for specific metrics. To be consistent with the estimand framework, we replaced “method of aggregation” with two distinct elements that describe values in individuals (rather than summary measures): “variable type” and “cutoff.” We further defined “cutoff” with three sub-elements, and we defined “variable type” as whether the value for each individual is continuous or categorical.

Conclusions

Trialists and sponsors could use this framework and guidance to define outcomes in trial registrations, protocols, and results reports. When all six elements are defined, readers can better determine whether reported outcomes were prespecified and whether different trials assessed the same outcomes.

entry.content:
by Joshua Dawe, Khadimul Anam Mazhar, Saher Aijaz Khan, Belinda Jackson Njiro, Victoria Bendaud, Keith Sabin, Julie Ambia, Adam Trickey, Lucy Barrass, Asra Asgharzadeh, Jack Stone, Adelina Artenie, Peter Vickerman

Background

Female sex workers (FSW) are a key population for HIV prevention and care. Increasing evidence suggests that social and structural barriers are key drivers of HIV transmission. This global systematic review assesses whether experiencing violence is associated with worse HIV outcomes among FSW.

Methods and findings

We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO databases for studies published from January 1st, 2010 to June 9th, 2026 assessing the impact of violence on HIV outcomes among FSW, without restriction to language and study design. Some studies had multiple estimates due to reporting on multiple outcomes or exposures of interest. We pooled data from eligible studies using multi-level random-effects meta-analyses to quantify associations between recent (past year) or lifetime exposure to violence (physical, sexual, emotional/psychological, and/or financial) and HIV outcomes (prevalent and incident HIV infection, HIV testing, ART use, ART adherence, and viral suppression) among FSW. We preferentially used adjusted estimates over unadjusted estimates if both were available.We included 94 studies with 226 estimates, comprising 186,613 FSWs in 39 countries. Half the included studies were in low- and middle-income countries (n = 47, 50%), and one-fifth were in low-income countries (n = 18; 19%). We found higher odds of prevalent HIV infection among FSWs with recent (pooled odds ratio (pOR):1.31; 95% CI [1.16,1.48]; I2: 63%; n = 75 estimates) and lifetime (pOR:1.35; 95% CI [1.23,1.48]; I2: 39%; n = 68) experiences of violence. When stratifying violence by type, we found the strongest pooled associations between recent (pOR:1.55; 95% CI [1.24,1.94]; I2: 69%; n = 28) and lifetime (pOR:1.40; 95% CI [1.21,1.63]; I2: 47%; n = 28) experiences of sexual violence and HIV prevalence. Recently experiencing violence was associated with reduced odds of ART use (pOR:0.78; 95% CI [0.64,0.94]; I2: 8%; n = 17). Lifetime exposure to violence was associated with reduced odds of viral suppression (pOR:0.88; 95% CI [0.79,0.98]; I2: 20%; n = 6). There was no evidence of associations between violence and HIV incidence, HIV testing, and ART adherence.Our study had limitations, notably the cross-sectional design of most included studies, the heterogeneity in pooled estimates, and the difficulties of measuring experiences of violence.

Conclusions

Experiencing violence is associated with greater odds of prevalent HIV infections, and poorer HIV treatment outcomes among FSWs. HIV interventions for FSWs must address violence as a structural determinant of HIV.

entry.content:
by Avnika B. Amin, Maria Garcia Quesada, Daniel Trudell, Natalie E. Dean, Benjamin A. Lopman, James A. Platts-Mills, Elizabeth T. Rogawski McQuade

Background

Effective vaccines against Shigella, the leading bacterial cause of diarrheal disease globally, could prevent morbidity and mortality from shigellosis as well as limit antibiotic resistance. Several Shigella vaccine candidates are in late stages of development, and the design of large Phase 3 trials in target populations is underway. In high incidence settings, children are expected to rapidly accrue natural immunity such that after repeated pathogen exposure, unvaccinated infants may have similar levels of immunity as vaccinated infants. For this reason, in these settings estimates of vaccine efficacy (VE) may underestimate expected efficacy in a fully naïve population. To set expectations and support optimal planning of future Shigella vaccine trials, we aimed to quantify the potential impact of this phenomenon on VE estimates under different surveillance strategies and assumptions about Shigella immunity.

Methods and findings

We simulated Shigella vaccine trials in low-, medium-, and high-burden settings under different assumptions about vaccine- and infection-conferred immunity. We estimated VE against severe, Shigella-attributable disease and any Shigella-attributable diarrhea under six trial designs: active surveillance for Shigella infection or symptom-based reporting paired with single-outcome, stratified recurrent outcome, or crude recurrent-outcome Cox proportional hazards models. In each scenario, we evaluated bias, 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, and the false negative rate. Only the trial design using active surveillance for infection and single outcome models was consistently unbiased across all examined scenarios. The other five designs underestimated VE by up to an absolute 20%, with a single outcome model paired with symptom-based reporting performing least poorly. Bias generally was worse at higher-burden sites. For realistically sized trials, the 95% CI coverage and false negative rate were also worse at higher-burden sites. The results were sensitive to input parameters which depended on assumptions about Shigella natural history based on limited published data.

Conclusions

The observed VE in Shigella vaccine trials is likely to underestimate true VE, though the magnitude of underestimation described here is conditional on the simulation’s inputs and assumptions. Careful trial design is needed to minimize this underestimation.

by Yani Huang, Ruixin Gao, Jianxin Li, Bin Yang, Keyong Huang, Shufeng Chen, Jie Cao, Xiaoqing Liu, Chong Shen, Ling Yu, Liancheng Zhao, Ying Li, Dongsheng Hu, Jianfeng Huang, Bin Lu, Dongfeng Gu, Fangchao Liu, Xiangfeng Lu

Background

Existing risk stratification tools inadequately identify individuals with subclinical atherosclerosis (SA) who could benefit from early intervention. This study aimed to develop protein risk scores (ProtRSs) for SA progression and assess their incremental value for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk prediction.

Methods and findings

In a community cohort consisting of 903 individuals undergoing repeated SA assessments (coronary artery calcium [CAC] or carotid plaque) over 6 years (2008–2009 to 2013–2014), protein biomarkers were selected from a panel of 117 proteins using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression to construct SA ProtRSs for CAC and plaque progression, respectively, and their predictive abilities for incident ASCVD risk were evaluated based on a guideline-recommended traditional risk score in a case-cohort of 1,835 individuals (2007–2008 to 2018–2021, median follow-up of 10.4 years). The ProtRSs each included 14 proteins for CAC and plaque progression, explaining 17.1% and 18.4% of respective variances. Effect sizes of these proteins on SA progression showed strong concordance with those on incident ASCVD (r  > 0.75). Each standard deviation increase in CAC and plaque ProtRSs was associated with hazard ratios of 1.36 (95% confidence interval [CI] [1.20,1.54]) and 1.38 (95% CI [1.23,1.54]) for ASCVD risk, respectively. Addition of the SA ProtRSs to the traditional risk score yielded a net reclassification improvement of 0.127 (p < 0.001). Importantly, 18.6% of traditional intermediate-risk individuals were reclassified into the high-risk category (10-year ASCVD event rate: 10.9%), indicating the need for preventive interventions, whereas 32.8% of traditional high-risk individuals were identified as having an even higher rate (13.7%), suggesting the requirement for intensified management. The main limitation is that the predictive value of ProtRSs warrants further large-scale external validation.

Conclusions

SA ProtRSs of coronary calcification and carotid plaque progression may provide additional value over traditional risk assessment, highlighting their potential in refining risk stratification and guiding targeted intervention strategies.

entry.content:
by Dana Pisică, Ana Mikolić, John K. Yue, Michael A. McCrea, Kristen Dams-O’Connor, Véronique De Keyser, Sonia Jain, Amy J. Markowitz, David K. Menon, Virginia Newcombe, Ewout W. Steyerberg, Xiaoying Sun, Hester F. Lingsma, Geoffrey T. Manley, Andrew I. R. Maas, on behalf of the CENTER-TBI and TRACK-TBI Investigators

Background

The CBI-M Framework, incorporating Clinical, Biomarker, Imaging, and Modifier pillars, was recently proposed to provide a comprehensive characterization of patients with acute traumatic brain injury (TBI). Such detailed characterization reflects the clinical and biological heterogeneity of TBI, and is considered essential to inform appropriate clinical management. Still unclear is the extent to which CBI-M captures clinically relevant heterogeneity in relation to diagnosis, clinical care pathways, and longer-term outcome. Prior to broad implementation into clinical practice and research, its diagnostic and prognostic performance needs to be ascertained. In this study, we aim to explore how CBI-M and its constituent pillars relate to diagnosis, clinical care pathways, and outcome in two large contemporary TBI cohorts.

Methods and findings

We analyzed data of patients with acute TBI enrolled in the European-based CENTER-TBI (N = 4,509) and US-based TRACK-TBI (N = 2,552) prospective observational studies. We assessed associations of the CBI-M Framework, its pillars, and pillar components with key clinical endpoints: diagnosis (traumatic intracranial injury on computed tomography); care pathways (hospital admission, intensive care admission, intracranial pressure monitoring, and major cranial surgery); and outcomes at 6 months post-injury (mortality, Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE), and health-related quality of life (HRQoL)). Discriminatory performance was calculated using the AUC and explained variability expressed with Nagelkerke’s pseudo-R2. Prognostic performance was compared to the established IMPACT-Lab and CRASH-CT prediction models in their respective target populations. For diagnostic and care path endpoints full CBI-M models achieved excellent discrimination (AUC CENTER-TBI: from 0.83 to 0.95; TRACK-TBI: from 0.88 to 0.98), and high proportions of explained variability (pseudo-R2 CENTER-TBI: from 0.41 to 0.72; TRACK-TBI: from 0.55 to 0.80). Contributions of individual pillars varied by endpoint, with the Biomarker pillar contributing most for CT-defined abnormalities and the Imaging pillar to major cranial surgery. For mortality and unfavorable outcome (GOSE ≤ 4) similarly strong performance was observed: CENTER-TBI: AUC 0.89 (95% Confidence intervals (CI) [0.88,0.90]) and 0.92 (95% CI [0.91,0.94]) respectively; pseudo-R2 0.53 (95% CI [0.50,0.57]) and 0.55 (95% CI [0.51,0.59]) respectively; TRACK-TBI: AUC 0.91 (95% CI [0.89,0.93]) and 0.95 (95% CI [0.93,0.97]) respectively; pseudo-R2 0.57 (95% CI [0.52,0.62] and 0.57 (95% CI [0.50, 0.64] respectively), whereas performance for HRQoL was modest. Compared to the IMPACT-Lab and CRASH-CT models in their respective target populations, pseudo-R2 values suggest that the full CBI-M model was more strongly associated with 6-month mortality and unfavorable outcomes. Methodological limitations include the restriction to analysis of data from high-income settings, limiting generalizability, the absence of three elements of the modifier pillar in the datasets accessed, and risk of possible reverse causality in some analyses.

Conclusions

CBI-M provides a robust multimodal characterization of acute TBI that aligns closely with clinical decision-making and outcomes. Further prospective validation and optimization are justified and needed to inform implementation of the CBI-M Framework in clinical practice and research.

by Ieuan Scanlon, Anna Rawlings, David Tucker, Daniel S. Thayer, Hywel T. Evans, Joanne Given, Sam Jones, Maria Loane, Chloe Morgan, Joan K. Morris, Sue Jordan

Background

Education outcomes are associated with life chances. However, deprivation, ill-health and disability are barriers to achievement. We aimed to investigate educational attainment of children with and without major congenital anomalies in state-funded mainstream schools at ages 11 and 16 (key stages [KS] 2 and 4), accounting for maternal and child socioeconomic deprivation, demographic factors, comorbidities, and special education needs (SEN) provision.

Methods and findings

We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using the Secure Anonymised Information Linkage (SAIL) Databank to link routinely collected electronic health and education records of children born in Wales between January 1st, 1998 and December 31st, 2007, who were followed up until December 31st, 2019. Education outcomes were explored using logistic regression, adjusting for: major congenital anomalies, maternal and child socioeconomic deprivation, medicated co-morbidities, hospitalisation, gestation length, child sex, year of birth, and SEN provision.Children with major congenital anomalies were less likely to achieve national academic standards, including those required for some professional courses: however, attainment was more strongly associated with socioeconomic deprivation. At age 11, 81.9% (7167/8754) with and 93.8% (232,450/247,814) without major congenital anomalies attained established standards (odds ratio [OR] 0.30; 95% confidence intervals [CI] [0.28,0.32]). At age 16, 46.8% (2070/4427) with and 56.1% (69,732/124,300) without major congenital anomalies achieved 5 General Certificates of Secondary Education (GCSEs) at grades C–A*, including English/Welsh, Maths and Science (EWMS) (OR 0.69; 95% CI [0.65,0.73]). Discrepancies narrowed in adjusted analyses, particularly when SEN provision was accounted: aOR 0.72; 95% CI [0.66,0.78] at KS2, age 11, and aOR 0.93; 95% CI [0.87,1.00] for 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS. These GCSEs were achieved by 29.7% (307/1034) children with major congenital anomalies and 38.4% (10,875/28,305) of unaffected children in the most deprived quintile (using maternal Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation: in the least deprived quintile, figures were 67.6% (547/810) and 75.0% (16,978/22,644), respectively.Children with major congenital anomalies, receiving maximum SEN support, and eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) were the least likely to achieve national academic standards: 5/192 (2.6%) obtained 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS, as did 37/354 (10.4%) ineligible for FSM. The strongest associations with 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS, were SEN statements (aOR 0.07; 95% CI [0.06,0.07]), FSM eligibility (aOR 0.39; 95% CI [0.37,0.41]), and epilepsy (aOR 0.60; 95% CI [0.45,0.80]). Study limitations included absence of data for 15%–18% of children, mainly those educated outside mainstream schools, and for some comorbidities; generalisation of findings to other settings or other countries is uncertain.

Conclusions

Many children with major congenital anomalies from least deprived quintiles attained national academic standards, including 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS. The children living in the most deprived quintiles or eligible for FSM and with ill-health from major congenital anomalies and/or epilepsy were two to four times less likely to attain these standards. SEN provision mitigated the associations with disadvantage, but children from socioeconomically deprived quintiles with major congenital anomalies were unlikely to achieve 5 GCSEs C–A* with EWMS.

by Leila Abar, Caitlin P. O’Connell, Hyokyoung G. Hong, Kirsten A. Herrick, Lisa Kahle, Jennifer L. Lerman, Linda M. Liao, Xuehong Zhang, Xinyuan Zhang, Longgang Zhao, Sémi Zouiouich, Rashmi Sinha, Neha Khandpur, Eurídice Martínez Steele, Erikka Loftfield

Background

Ultra-processed foods (UPF) account for >50% of energy intake by US adults. UPF intake can include dietary components linked to lower colorectal cancer (CRC) risk, such as whole grain and dairy products, and others linked to higher CRC risk, such as processed meats, potentially explaining the heterogeneity of evidence for an association between UPF and CRC risk. Our goal was to estimate the associations of UPF and established CRC-related dietary factors, by UPF and non-UPF source, with CRC incidence in a large cohort study.

Methods and findings

US adults, aged 50–71, who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study in 1995–96, self-reported dietary intake using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). Median UPF intake was 293 g/1000 kcal/day or 43% of daily energy intake. We assigned disaggregated FFQ items to Nova classification and categorized UPF intake (g/1000 kcal/day) into sex-specific quintiles. Participants who were cancer-free at baseline (N = 461,682) were followed for cancer incidence through 2018, and 10,075 colorectal adenocarcinoma cases were diagnosed. We used multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards regression models, adjusted for demographic, lifestyle, and health-related factors, including age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, physical activity, smoking, and alcohol drinking, to estimate associations for UPF and related dietary components with CRC incidence. UPF intake was not associated with CRC incidence (hazard ratio 5th versus 1st quintile 0.97; 95% confidence interval [0.91–1.03]; ptrend = 0.55). Whole grain, fiber, dairy, and calcium intakes from UPF sources were inversely but meat intake from UPF sources was positively associated with CRC incidence. The main limitations of the study relate to its observational design and include potential residual confounding and exposure misclassification owing to systematic or random error in self-reported dietary data.

Conclusions

Total UPF intake was not associated with incident CRC in this cohort of older, US adults. This may be explained, in part, by opposing associations of some UPF with CRC risk. Our findings support current dietary guidance to consume whole grains, fiber, dairy, and calcium and avoid processed meat for CRC prevention.

by Catherine G. C. Wenger, Kyra H. Grantz, Tigist F. Menkir, Alina M. Muellenmeister, Zeaan Pithawala, Raymond Hutubessy, Vittal Mogasale, Alicia N. M. Kraay, Nick Scott, Romesh G. Abeysuriya, Jason R. Andrews, Jillian Gauld, Nathan C. Lo, Virginia E. Pitzer

Background

Given emerging evidence on the waning of immunity from typhoid conjugate vaccines (TCV), the World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned a multi-model comparison to determine the optimal schedule in terms of health and economic impact to inform updated recommendations for TCV use across different settings.

Methods and findings

To identify optimal vaccination strategies across different incidence settings and vaccine waning assumptions, we compared two agent-based and two compartmental dynamic models of typhoid transmission. All models were fitted to harmonized age-specific incidence data from medium, high, and very high incidence settings. We assessed different TCV schedules under slow- and fast-waning scenarios to evaluate the best age for routine vaccination and the potential need for booster doses and catch-up campaigns. We evaluated the public health and economic impact predicted for each model and scenario using the net-monetary-benefit framework to determine cost-effectiveness under two representative scenarios for the health outcomes and costs of vaccination and treatment. Over a 10-year time horizon, routine vaccination at 9 months with a catch-up campaign to 15 years and a booster dose at 5 years was predicted to have the greatest impact, reducing cases by a median of 40%–68% across the incidence settings. Across all four models, TCV introduction with a catch-up campaign was cost-effective above willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds of $1,250 per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted in medium incidence settings when costs of illness and case fatality risk (CFR) are high and in high incidence settings when costs and CFR are low. The optimal strategy was to delay vaccination to 2 or 5 years of age if waning is fast, depending on the age of peak incidence. In very high incidence settings, TCV introduction at 9 months or 2 years of age was cost-saving, and adding a booster dose at 5 years was cost-effective at most WTP values across all scenarios. The study findings are limited by the data available to inform indirect vaccine protection and other simplifying assumptions made in this analysis.

Conclusions

Model predictions for the impact and cost-effectiveness of different TCV schedules were fairly robust to uncertainty in parameter values and model structure, but the optimal strategy depends on the typhoid incidence rate, CFR, and waning rate of vaccine protection.

by Hyeon Jin Kim, Yesol Yim, Christa J. Nehs, Jaeyu Park, Eun Soo Kim, Sung Joon Cho, Guillaume Fond, Laurent Boyer, Jiseung Kang, Dong Keon Yon

Background

Prenatal opioid exposure may disrupt infant development and immune system function, potentially increasing long-term susceptibility to hospital admissions. Thus, we aimed to investigate the association between prenatal opioid exposure and the risk of hospital admission in children.

Methods and findings

We established a population-based birth cohort in South Korea by linking mothers and children using National Health Insurance Service data and followed from January 1, 2009, to December 31, 2023. We constructed propensity score (PS)-matched and sibling comparison cohorts and performed a multi-pronged approach, including dose-dependent and time-attenuation analyses. All 5,249,429 individuals with eligible children born between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2017, were included (2,236,167 mothers and 3,013,262 children). Infants were followed up for up to 14 years, depending on birth year. Prenatal exposure to opioids was defined as maternal receipt of two or more prescriptions within any given trimester. Adjusted incidence rate ratio (aIRR) of hospital admission among children with prenatal opioid exposure was estimated for causes including infections, non-infectious respiratory conditions, non-infectious gastrointestinal conditions, oral cavity diseases, injuries/external causes, and non-infectious genitourinary conditions. Analyses were adjusted for maternal age at delivery, infant sex, region of residence, household income level, birth season, parity, severe maternal morbidity score, number of outpatient visits and hospital admissions in the year before pregnancy, preterm birth, low birth weight, delivery type, year of delivery, maternal history of substance use and neuropsychiatric disorders, and plurality. Of the 2,928,186 children, we identified 2,809,515 (51.4% male) and 118,671 (51.3% male) infants without and with prenatal opioid exposure, respectively. The rate of hospital admissions in children with prenatal opioid exposure was 28% higher in the PS-matched cohort (aIRR 1.28 [95% CI 1.28, 1.29]; p < 0.001). The association was attenuated in the sibling comparison cohort, indicating the potential influence of shared familial factors, but remained statistically significant (aIRR 1.08 [95% CI 1.07, 1.10]; p < 0.001). Hospital admission rates in children increased in a dose-dependent manner with maternal opioid dose and duration of opioid prescriptions (low-dose exposure: aIRR 1.19 [95% CI 1.19, 1.20]; p < 0.001; high-dose exposure: aIRR 1.40 [95% CI 1.39, 1.41]; p < 0.001). Prenatal opioid exposure was significantly associated with increased rates of hospital admission across several causes of morbidities, including infections, respiratory non-infections, oral cavity, gastrointestinal non-infections, genitourinary non-infections, and injury/external conditions. These associations between prenatal opioid exposure and hospital admission rates in children diminished with age but remained evident up to five years of age. The main limitations of this study’s methodology include the use of prescription records, which may not fully capture actual medication intake, and residual confounding that cannot be entirely excluded.

Conclusions

In this nationwide birth cohort study, maternal opioid prescription during pregnancy was associated with a substantial increase in the risk of hospital admissions in the offspring across various causes of morbidities. Although the attenuated estimates in the sibling comparison analysis suggest that familial factors may partly explain this association, these findings may inform postnatal monitoring and management strategies for children born to mothers who received opioid prescriptions during pregnancy.

by Xinya Li, Xue Xia, Meng Gao, Qin Xu, Yijun Zhang, Jing Jing, Yi Zhai, Xia Meng, Anxin Wang

Background

Amlodipine and nifedipine are the most commonly prescribed calcium channel blockers (CCB) for patients suffering from ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA). Nevertheless, there is a scarcity of direct comparative evidence on their effectiveness. This study aimed to compare the effectiveness of amlodipine and nifedipine in patients with ischemic stroke or TIA.

Methods and findings

This observational study was based on the Third China National Stroke Registry, which recruited consecutive adult patients with ischemic stroke or TIA from 2015 to 2018. In this study, ischemic stroke or TIA patients were prescribed either amlodipine or nifedipine at discharge. The primary outcome was the distribution of modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score, which assesses functional outcomes in patients with stroke, at 5 years. The intergroup differences were examined using ordinal logistic regression, yielding odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Patient age, gender, body mass index, systolic blood pressure at admission, and onset date were adjusted. To improve baseline characteristic balance, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was implemented. A total of 2,859 eligible patients were included, and there were 1847 patients in the amlodipine group and 1,058 patients in the nifedipine group after IPTW. The amlodipine group demonstrated significantly lower 5-year mRS scores in comparison to the nifedipine group, with an OR of 0.76 (95% CI [0.65, 0.89]; p < 0.001). A total of 956 (51.76%) amlodipine users and 632 (59.74%) nifedipine users achieved a mRS score > 0 at 5 years, with an OR of 0.71 (95% CI [0.61, 0.83]; p < 0.001). The sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. The main limitations include the inherent observational design, the exclusive reliance on registry data, and relatively high loss-to-follow-up rate at 5 years.

Conclusions

This study revealed that amlodipine, compared to nifedipine, may be associated with improved functional recovery in ischemic stroke or TIA patients. Randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm these findings and refine CCB therapy.

entry.content:
by Yan Ning Li, Kumar S. D. Kothapalli, Susan E. Carlson, Byron J. Gajewski, Emily A. DeFranco, J. Thomas Brenna

Background

Spontaneous early preterm birth (EPB < 34 weeks) is a major contributor to newborn morbidity and mortality; it depends on ancestry, and preventive measures are limited. The insertion (I) allele of the fatty acid desaturase (FADS) Indel polymorphism (rs66698963) modulates FADS1 expression, and increases arachidonic acid synthesis, enhancing parturifacient prostaglandins. Omega-3 docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) inhibits this pathway. Whether FADS Indel genotype predicts response to DHA dose in pregnancy is unknown.

Methods and findings

To determine whether FADS Indel genotype modifies the effect of DHA dose on gestational length, we conducted a post hoc secondary analysis of the Assessment of DHA on Reducing Early Preterm Birth (ADORE) trial (NCT02626299). The FADS Indel, the only genetic variant measured, was selected on mechanistic grounds and genotyped blind to outcome. The analysis included all participants consenting to genetic analysis (12–20 weeks gestation) at three US medical centers. Participants received 200 or 1,000 mg/d DHA and were genotyped for FADS Indel (D/D, I/D, I/I). Primary outcomes were EPB and preterm birth (PB, <37 weeks) analyzed using treatment-specific Bayesian binomial models. Cervical length was assessed in 574 participants.Women (n = 10,497) were screened for eligibility from June 8th 2016, to March 13th 2020, 1,032 (1,000 mg, n = 540; 200 mg, n = 492) completed the ADORE trial. A total of 761 (1,000 mg, n = 396; 200 mg, n = 365) are included in this secondary analysis. Participants carrying at least one FADS Indel I allele (I/I + I/D) receiving low-dose DHA had 4.3% EPB (9/214; 95% Credible Interval (CrI) [2.0%, 7.3%]) versus 0.8% in the D/D group (1/151; 95% CrI [0.04%, 2.7%]; Posterior Probability (PP) = 0.99), and 14.5% PB (31/214; 95% CrI [10.1%, 19.5%]) versus 8.7% in the D/D group (13/151; 95% CrI [4.7%, 13.6%]; PP = 0.96). High-dose DHA was associated with reduced EPB in the I-allele group (1.1%; 2/205; 95% CrI [0.2%, 2.8%]; PP = 0.99), and PB (9.3%; 19/205; 95% CrI [5.7%, 13.6%]; PP = 0.95), with little effect in the D/D group. Birth at ≥40 weeks was more frequent in the high-dose D/D group. Black women had higher rates of PB and EPB, have higher rates of the I allele, and benefited most from 1,000 mg/d dose. These dose effects credibly differ by genotype for EPB and prolonged gestation (genotype × dose interaction PP = 0.99 and 0.98). Both genotypes reduced PB similarly with high-dose DHA (PP = 0.56). Although genetic analysis was anticipated and genotyping was completed blind to outcome, this was a post hoc analysis and the genotype-by-dose comparison was not a prespecified trial aim. Some subgroups contained few PB and EPB events, so these estimates, particularly for PB, should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed prospectively.

Conclusions

The FADS Indel is a functional, mechanistically grounded polymorphism whose frequency varies with race/ethnicity. Preterm and early preterm birth were lower in the I-allele group receiving high-dose DHA (1,000 mg/d), while prolonged gestation was more frequent in the D/D group receiving high-dose DHA. FADS Indel genotypes predicted the direction of the response to high-dose DHA for EPB and prolonged gestation, whereas its modest PB benefit was shared by both genotypes. Analysis by retrospectively pairing high dose to I-carrier genotype and low dose to D/D was associated with the highest proportion of births at 37–40 weeks. These findings identify the FADS Indel as a potential predictive biomarker for DHA dose response and support a genotype-informed, precision-medicine strategy to optimize gestational length by reducing preterm birth in the I-allele group and prolonged gestation in the D/D group across racially/ethnically diverse populations.

Trial registration

entry.content:
by Sun Kim, Melike Hazal Can, Hannah M. Rickman, Mphatso D. Phiri, Marriott Nliwasa, Tisungane E. Mwenyenkulu, Kuzani Mbendera, Stéphane Verguet, Marcia C. Castro, Elizabeth L. Corbett, Peter MacPherson, Ted Cohen, Nicolas A. Menzies

Background

Active case finding (ACF) for tuberculosis (TB) can reduce transmission, yet efficient targeting requires high-quality surveillance data. We investigated the potential costs and impact of targeted ACF, guided by local estimates of the annual risk of TB infection (ARTI) derived from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) immunoreactivity survey data in children aged <5 years.

Methods and findings

Using mathematical models parameterized with local data, we compared three case-finding approaches across 33 urban neighborhoods in Blantyre, Malawi: passive case finding (PCF) only; PCF with untargeted ACF; and PCF with ARTI-guided targeted ACF. Health outcomes (life expectancy, disability-adjusted life years [DALYs]) and costs were estimated using a Markov microsimulation model. Costs were assessed from health system and societal perspectives. Results were calculated for different assumptions about the relationship between ARTI and true TB prevalence.Compared to PCF-only, untargeted ACF was estimated to improve life expectancy by 3.3 years (95% credible interval (CrI) [1.7, 5.4]) for individuals with TB disease, but at high cost. Targeted ACF covering half of the study population was estimated to identify 80% of all individuals with TB and achieved a lower cost per DALY averted (US$400, 95% CrI [20,1,000]) than untargeted ACF (US$700, 95% CrI [100, 1,500]). In the main analysis, these cost-effectiveness ratios exceeded available cost-effectiveness thresholds for Malawi, although cost-effectiveness improved under assumptions of higher TB prevalence or greater transmission reduction. The findings are based on mathematical modeling and are subject to several limitations, including assumptions regarding the relationship between ARTI and TB prevalence, which remains uncertain.

Conclusions

Targeting ACF using Mtb immunoreactivity survey data could substantially improve health impact and cost-effectiveness compared to untargeted approaches. However, low-cost approaches for collecting these data are needed for wider adoption.

entry.content:
by Zhengyang Zhu, Kejun Ren, Dong Wang, Yong Lv, Hua Jin, Lei Zhang, Yiping Wang

Background

The cardiovascular‑kidney‑metabolic (CKM) syndrome shows substantial heterogeneity in progression, yet existing biological age indices are not tailored to CKM pathways. We developed an aging index (CKMAI) using machine learning and evaluated its predictive performance for mortality and high‑risk CKM status.

Methods and findings

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 6,896 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2005–2018, weighted for the US adult population. A two‑stage machine learning framework evaluated over 100 candidate survival models; the optimal model was selected via Pareto front optimization. Predictive performance was assessed using time‑dependent area under the curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Nonlinear relationships and threshold effects were examined with restricted cubic splines and two‑piecewise regression. Additive interactions were quantified by relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) and attributable proportion (AP). Unsupervised clustering identified aging‑metabolic phenotypes. Weighted bootstrap mediation analysis assessed the mediating role of depression.The Pareto‑optimal simple Cox model achieved a mean C‑index of 0.893. CKMAI consistently outperformed PhenoAge, KDM, and the cardiometabolic index (CMI) across all outcomes. For all‑cause mortality, CKMAI’s time‑dependent AUCs were 0.893 (95% CI [0.851, 0.925]) at 3 years, 0.907 (95% CI [0.884, 0.927]) at 5 years, and 0.890 (95% CI [0.868, 0.910]) at 10 years; for cardiovascular mortality, 0.904 (95% CI [0.840, 0.943]), 0.937 (95% CI [0.892, 0.960]), and 0.937 (95% CI [0.900, 0.959]); for high‑risk CKM status, 0.790 (95% CI [0.765, 0.816]). NRI and IDI were significant at all time points (P < 0.05 for all), calibration was good (Greenwood‑Nam‑D’Agostino test P > 0.05), and DCA confirmed superior net benefit. Nonlinear associations were found for all three outcomes. Threshold analysis identified inflection points at CKMAI 61.587 (all‑cause mortality), 60.732 (cardiovascular mortality), and 34.092 (high‑risk CKM status), with steeper risk increases below each threshold. CKMAI exhibited super‑additive interactions with PhenoAge (RERI 15.06, 95% CI [8.14, 38.44]). Clustering revealed six distinct aging‑metabolic phenotypes; the frail elderly cluster had the highest mortality risk (hazard ratio [HR] 11.74, 95% CI [7.85, 17.57]). Depression partially mediated the CKMAI‑outcome associations (proportions mediated: 5.6% [95% CI 2.3%–9.0%] for all‑cause mortality, 8.2% [95% CI 2.8%–22.0%] for cardiovascular mortality, 11.1% [95% CI 6.7%–24.0%] for high‑risk CKM status). Findings were robust across prespecified subgroups and multiple sensitivity analyses. A key limitation is the lack of validation in geographically independent cohorts with complete mortality follow-up; however, temporal validation within NHANES and preliminary external validation in a hospital based Chinese cohort (n = 261) supported the generalizability of the CKMAI for identifying high risk CKM status.

Conclusions

CKMAI is a valid, CKM‑specific aging index that outperforms universal biological age measures in predicting mortality and identifying high‑risk CKM status. Its super‑additive interactions with PhenoAge and the partial mediation by depression offer new mechanistic insights into CKM heterogeneity. By integrating a diverse set of clinical laboratory measures, nutritional assessments, lifestyle factors, and social determinants of health, CKMAI provides a practical, implementable tool for risk stratification and targeted prevention in CKM syndrome.

entry.content:
by Maureen Moyo-Chilufya, Arthemon Nguweneza, Sara Rotenberg, Hannah Kuper, Tracey Smythe

Background

Mortality is a fundamental marker of population health and equity. Despite major global declines in mortality over recent decades, disparities in survival persist across childhood and adolescence, particularly by disability status. We aimed to synthesise current evidence on all-cause mortality among children and adolescents with disabilities compared to their non-disabled peers through a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Methods and findings

This review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251072039). We searched Embase, Global Health, MEDLINE, PubMed and PsycInfo to identify relevant studies published from January 1, 2000 to August 20, 2026. We included cohort studies that compared all-cause mortality rates for children and adolescents with and without disabilities (aged 0–19 years). We excluded studies without a clear definition of disability, disaggregated mortality data, or a control group. Two authors independently screened studies, with data extraction by one and verification by a second. We assessed risk of bias using a Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool. We conducted meta-analyses in RevMan for studies reporting age-sex-adjusted or multivariable-adjusted mortality ratios and R software to assess for publication bias. We reported heterogeneity using the I2 and τ2 statistics. We identified 12,664 records of which 29 studies met the inclusion criteria, representing over 35 million children/adolescents. Sixteen studies were eligible to be included in the meta-analysis. Overall, children with disabilities had a 5.31-fold (95% confidence interval (CI) [3.63,7.77]; p < 0.001; τ2 = 0.88; I2 = 98%) higher all-cause mortality than their peers. The association between disability and mortality was higher in both younger children 0–5 years (Hazard ratio (HR)=7.51: 95%CI [4.70,12.00]; p < 0.001; τ2 = 0.44; I2 = 91%) and children 6–19 years (HR = 4.68: 95%CI [2.26,9.69]; p < 0.001; τ2 = 0.93; I2 = 96%). The association varied by disability type and was most stark for children with neurological disabilities (HR = 11.71: 95%CI [7.90,17.35]; p < 0.001; τ2 = 0.19; I2 = 76%). Interpretation is limited by substantial between-study heterogeneity, differences in methods used to ascertain disability ascertainment and in the effect measures used, and the small number of studies from low-income and middle-income countries.

Conclusions

Children with disabilities experience substantially higher mortality than their peers without disabilities. There is an urgent need for evidence on what works to close the mortality gap.

entry.content:
by Po-Huang Chen, Ming-Shen Dai, Mao-Hsuan Huang, Hsin-Yu Chen, Li-Ting Kao, Tina Yi-Jin Hsieh, Hong-Jie Jhou, Cho-Hao Lee

Background

Preclinical evidence identifies the serotonin transporter (SERT, encoded by SLC6A4) as an immune checkpoint on CD8+ T cells, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) enhancing antitumor immunity in synergy with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy. Whether this translates into clinical benefit for patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is unknown. Using a target trial emulation framework, we compared outcomes between SSRI users and benzodiazepine (BZD) users among patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving an ICI. Separately, in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which covers a different set of patients, we examined how SLC6A4 expression related to tumor immune-cell infiltration across cancers.

Methods and findings

We emulated a target trial in the TriNetX federated electronic health record network (over 187 million patients), comparing SSRI with BZD treatment at first ICI administration under an intention-to-treat-analogue estimand. Eligible patients were adults with a solid tumor, a first ICI administration between 2015 and 2025, and a depressive or anxiety disorder recorded within the prior 365 days. Exposure required an active SSRI or BZD prescription overlapping the index date or starting within the preceding 90 days, not necessarily on that date. The primary outcome was 2-year overall survival; 20 secondary outcomes across 4 mechanistic pathways were prespecified. Propensity score matching (1:1) on 49 baseline covariates yielded 1,567 pairs. Estimates are hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Transcriptomic analyses used TCGA (8,272 tumor samples from 8,172 patients, 20 tumor types). Among 3,134 matched patients, SSRI use was associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality (23.5% versus 34.4%; HR 0.627; 95% CI [0.549, 0.716]; p < 0.001; E-value 2.57). Composite immune-related adverse events (irAEs) were more frequent with SSRI use (HR 1.162; 95% CI [1.039, 1.299]; p = 0.008), driven by thyroid dysfunction (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), without increases in hepatitis, pneumonitis, or colitis (all p > 0.09). Newly coded distant metastases were less frequent in the SSRI group (HR 0.629; 95% CI [0.487, 0.811]; p < 0.001), and the 3 prespecified negative controls (nephrolithiasis, cholelithiasis, cataract) showed null associations (all p > 0.76). All 5 individually analyzable SSRIs were associated with lower mortality (HR range 0.61 to 0.71). In TCGA, SLC6A4 expression was inversely correlated with T-cell inflammation in 13 of 20 cancer types, and this organ-level pattern matched that of organ-specific irAEs. The main limitation is residual confounding: performance status, a clinician’s rating of everyday functional ability that strongly predicts cancer survival, is not recorded in the network, and BZDs are prescribed in different circumstances from SSRIs, so the groups may differ in ways matching cannot capture. The TCGA analyses used bulk tumor tissue from patients not treated with ICIs, so they cannot localize SLC6A4 to particular cells or show that SSRIs alter the tumor microenvironment.

Conclusions

In this study, SSRI use was associated with lower mortality and organ-selective immune activation compared with BZD use among ICI-treated patients with psychiatric comorbidity. Transcriptomic evidence supports biological plausibility. These findings warrant prospective evaluation of SSRI repurposing as an ICI adjuvant.
